facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Allahabad Fort. Ashokan Pillar (Inscribed stone pillar). Zanana Palace. Prayagraj.
facts.text: The monumental sandstone Allahabad Fort was constructed in 1583 CE by Emperor Akbar at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna rivers and is documented as a centrally protected monument by the Archaeological Survey of India.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Allahabad Fort: Ashoka Pillar (Inscribed stone pillar), Prayagraj, Near Sangam, Prayagraj
facts.text: An epigraphic survey by the Archaeological Survey of India confirmed that the Ashokan Pillar standing within the fort complex contains 3rd-century BCE Mauryan edicts and the 4th-century CE Prayag Prashasti of Samudragupta.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Excavations at Sringaverapura in Allahabad have provided a cultural sequence from about the 11th century bce till medieval times, but the significance of the site lies in the massive Kushan-period burnt-brick tank and its elaborate inlet channel with intercommunicating system and terraced sides.
facts.text: Systematic excavations conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India between 1977 and 1986 CE at nearby Sringaverapura in Prayagraj revealed an ancient monumental brick-built tank and hydraulic engineering works along the Ganga.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: He slew the demon Mahīrāvaṇa and brought Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa from his place to their own after guarding them well.
facts.text: The Shiva Purana states that Hanuman descended to Patala to slay the demon Mahiravana and securely bring back Rama and Lakshmana.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: As per the mythology, Lord Hanuman rested here after setting afire Lanka as per the epic Ramayana.
facts.text: According to local tradition, Hanuman was exhausted after the war of Lanka and the conquest of Ahiravana, choosing to rest in a reclining position on the banks of the Sangam at Sita's request.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: According to legend, a wealthy but childless businessman from Kannauj commissioned an idol of Hanuman from stones found in the Vindhyachal hills. After leaving the idol at Prayagraj during his pilgrimage to the Triveni Sangam, he was blessed with a son.
facts.text: Local folklore tells of a childless merchant from Kannauj who carved a colossal Hanuman statue out of Vindhyachal rock and was told in a dream to leave it in Prayag, after which he was blessed with a son.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The idol was later discovered by Baba Balagiri Ji Maharaj while preparing a dhuni (sacred site for worship) and was installed at its current location.
facts.text: Temple lore recounts that the ascetic Baba Balagiri Ji Maharaj rediscovered the submerged idol while digging a sacred fire trench and established the modern shrine.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Akbar attempted to move the idol, but despite using dozens of elephants, the statue did not budge.
facts.text: A popular local story claims that Emperor Akbar attempted to shift the monumental statue using war elephants during fort construction, but failed when the idol could not be budged.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Devotees consider the annual phenomenon of the bathing of the idol of Lord Hanuman by Ganga very auspicious and lucky for the city.
facts.text: Pilgrims believe that monsoon floodwaters entering the subterranean sanctum represent Goddess Ganga arriving to bathe Hanuman's feet before the river begins to recede.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The idol in the Temple is in the supine position or veer-mudra.
facts.text: Scholars and temple traditionalists disagree on whether the monumental carving was sculpted deliberately in a reclining sleep posture or represents an upright warrior combat stela that came to lie horizontally after tilting into river silt.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The temple's origins date back approximately 700 years.
facts.text: While monastic tradition dates the idol's installation to roughly 700 years ago, art historians argue that monumental reliefs depicting Hanuman crushing Ahiravana flourished in North India primarily during the Ramanandi Bhakti movement between the 16th and 18th centuries CE.
